progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c08a (primary alcohol oxidised under reflux to a carboxylic acid; ethanoic acid named); chem-m7-c08b (the carbonyl group, polar C=O, dipole–dipole forces, the boiling point strip); chem-m7-c05 (alcohol naming, hydrogen bonding from an O–H, donor and acceptor, propan-1-ol 97 °C, "Same size? Hydrogen bonding wins. Same family? Size wins.", solubility falling with chain length); chem-m7-c03 (dispersion forces, the water lattice); chem-m7-c01 (naming rules, locants, branches); chem-m6-c01 (proton transfer, H₃O⁺); chem-m6-c02 (acid with hydroxide, metal and carbonate; carbonic acid breaks into water and CO₂); chem-m6-c05 (weak means partial ionisation; weak is not dilute; ethanoic acid at 0.10 mol/L pH 2.9, about 1 in 80); chem-m6-c10 (Ka, pKa, lower pKa is stronger, each unit a factor of 10, conjugate base). Not assumed: carboxyl group, "-oic acid" naming, dimer, carboxylate and ethanoate, the hydrogen carbonate test, why the conjugate base's charge matters.
progression.startsWith: Identify the carboxyl group and its intermolecular forces. The video opens: In the alcohol reactions video, ethanol was oxidised under reflux, all the way to ethanoic acid. That's the acid in vinegar. Now compare it with propan-one-ol.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying and drawing the carboxyl group; naming carboxylic acids up to C8 with methyl or ethyl branches; explaining their boiling points and solubility against other families and within the series; explaining why a carboxylic acid is a weak acid and an alcohol is not, using the conjugate base's shared charge and pKa; describing the litmus and hydrogen carbonate observations and writing the reactions with sodium hydroxide, magnesium and sodium hydrogen carbonate. No organic bases, no esters.

teaching.task: Ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol have the same molar mass, and both contain an O–H group. Yet the acid boils 21 degrees higher, turns blue litmus red and fizzes with baking soda, while the alcohol does none of these. What does the carboxyl group change, and why does it make the molecule an acid?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol have the same mass and both have an O–H, yet the acid boils 21 °C higher, turns litmus red and fizzes (1); (2) the carboxyl group is C=O and O–H on one carbon, only one O–H, both bonds polar (2); (3) names end "-oic acid"; the carboxyl carbon is C1 and counts in the chain (3); (4) alcohols also give and take hydrogen bonds, so that alone is not the difference; the C=O beside the O–H is a second taker, so the O–H gives and the C=O takes a hydrogen bond, and pairs lock with two (dimers), plus dipole–dipole forces, so the acid boils higher (4); (5) longer chains add dispersion, so boiling points climb; small acids mix with water and solubility falls after C4 (5); (6) in water the O–H hydrogen can transfer to water as H⁺, but the equilibrium lies well to the left, because ethanoate ions keep taking protons back: a weak acid (6); (7) the C=O beside the oxygen lets the charge left behind spread across two oxygens, about half on each, and half a charge pulls on a proton less strongly, so ethanoate takes protons back less readily; an alcohol has no C=O there, so its charge would sit on one oxygen; pKa 4.7 against 16 (7); (8) evidence: litmus, because the acid raises the hydronium ion concentration (8); (9) reactions as an acid, salts "-oate" (9); (10) the hydrogen carbonate test and why it works (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol have the same molar mass and both contain an O-H, yet the acid boils 21 degrees higher, turns blue litmus red and fizzes with baking soda, so the video asks what the carboxyl group changes and why it makes the molecule an acid. The carboxyl group is a C=O and an O-H on one carbon; names end in oic acid with the carboxyl carbon as carbon one. The O-H gives a hydrogen bond and the C=O oxygen takes one, so two acid molecules lock together as a dimer with two hydrogen bonds and boil higher than alcohols of similar size, and along the family each extra CH2 adds dispersion forces while small acids still mix with water. In water the O-H hydrogen can leave as a proton to make hydronium and an ethanoate ion, but the equilibrium lies well to the left and only about one molecule in eighty gives its proton away, so it is a weak acid (partly ionised, not dilute); it lets go because the ion left behind spreads its negative charge over two oxygens, while an alcohol's ion cannot. Litmus shows the raised hydronium, the acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide like a Module 6 acid, and sodium hydrogen carbonate gives carbon dioxide as the most useful test. The memory aid ranks similar-sized molecules: carboxylic acid above alcohol above aldehyde and ketone above alkane. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In the alcohol reactions video, ethanol was oxidised under reflux, all the way to ethanoic acid. That's the acid in vinegar. Now compare it with propan-one-ol. Both have a molar mass of sixty, and both contain an O H group. Yet the acid boils at one hundred and eighteen degrees, and the alcohol at ninety seven. The acid turns blue litmus red, and it fizzes with baking soda. The alcohol does neither. So what does the acid's group change?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Compound X has the condensed structural formula CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH and boils at 177 °C. Hexan-1-ol, which has a similar molar mass, boils at 157 °C. (a) Give the IUPAC name of X. (b) Explain why X has the higher boiling point, with reference to the intermolecular forces present." A skeletal formula of X is shown beside it in plain ink (no colours, no locants). New molecules (scenes use C1 to C4 straight chains and 2-methylpropanoic acid); tests counting the carboxyl carbon and the dimer reason. Crossed mistake: "2-methylpropanoic acid" (the carboxyl carbon left out of the chain, which names a different, smaller acid; the site's chain-length rule). (A2) "Butanoic acid and butan-1-ol are both colourless liquids. Describe a chemical test that would distinguish them, including a balanced equation for any reaction. Explain why only one of them reacts." New pair (scenes use ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol); tests the hydrogen carbonate test, the equation with CO₂, and the reason (a stronger acid than carbonic acid, because the conjugate base's charge is shared). Crossed mistake: "Both contain an O–H group, so both react." (the lesson's central misconception, L18 Q2 distractor pattern).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127); alkanes; alkenes; alkynes; alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary); aldehydes and ketones; carboxylic acids; amines and amides; halogenated organic compounds" This video covers carboxylic acids only (hydrocarbons chem-m7-c01 and g01; haloalkanes chem-m7-c04a; alcohols chem-m7-c05; aldehydes and ketones chem-m7-c08b; amines and amides chem-m7-c11). "investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including:; primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols; aldehydes and ketones (ACSCH127); amines and amides; carboxylic acids" This video covers carboxylic acids (alcohols chem-m7-c05; aldehydes and ketones chem-m7-c08b; amines and amides chem-m7-c11). "explain the properties within and between the homologous series of carboxylic acids amines and amides with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present" This video covers carboxylic acids, within their series and against alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and alkanes; amines and amides are chem-m7-c11. "investigate the differences between an organic acid and organic base" This video covers the organic acid: what makes a carboxylic acid acidic and how its acid behaviour is observed. The organic base and the comparison are chem-m7-c11 (route review change 3). this video starts by identifying the carboxyl group and its intermolecular forces, and stops at explaining why a carboxylic acid is a weak acid while an alcohol is not, with the observations that show it. It teaches: the carboxyl group (–COOH) is a carbonyl (C=O) and a hydroxyl (O–H) on the same carbon; the two oxygens differ, and there is only one O–H; inside the molecule the bonds are covalent, and both the C=O and the O–H are polar (the intramolecular part of `C7-IQ5-02`); naming (longest chain including the carboxyl carbon, drop the final "e", add "oic acid"; the carboxyl carbon is C1, so no locant; it is counted in the chain; branches numbered from it: 2-methylpropanoic acid); hydrogen bonding: the O–H donates and the C=O oxygen accepts, so two molecules can pair with two hydrogen bonds (a dimer), plus dipole–dipole forces from the C=O, so for similar sizes a carboxylic acid boils higher than an alcohol (ethanoic acid 118 °C against propan-1-ol 97 °C, both about 60 g/mol); within the series, boiling point rises with chain length (more dispersion), and solubility in water falls after butanoic acid; in water the O–H hydrogen can transfer to water as H⁺, forming H₃O⁺ and the carboxylate ion (ethanoate), but the reaction is reversible and the equilibrium lies well to the left, so only a small fraction ionises (weak, not dilute; Module 6 recall: pH about 2.9 at 0.10 mol/L, about 1 molecule in 80); why: the C=O beside the oxygen lets the charge left on the carboxylate spread across both oxygens, about half on each, so it does not take the proton back as strongly; an alkoxide has no C=O there, so its charge would sit on one oxygen; so pKa about 4.7 against about 16 (Module 6 recall: lower pKa, stronger acid; each unit a factor of 10); evidence: blue litmus turns red with the acid and stays blue with the alcohol; reactions as an acid (Module 6 recall): with sodium hydroxide (salt and water), with magnesium (salt and hydrogen), salts named "-oate"; the sodium hydrogen carbonate test: the acid is stronger than carbonic acid, so it gives a proton to hydrogen carbonate, and the carbonic acid breaks up into water and CO₂, so it fizzes; an alcohol does not; the equation includes CO₂. Not here: the organic base and the acid against base comparison (chem-m7-c11, route review change 3); amines and amides; esters and esterification (chem-m7-c10, next); phenol (beyond the 2017 syllabus; the site marks it as extension; author note f); chloroethanoic acid and inductive effects (author note f); pH or Ka calculations (Module 6); salt hydrolysis and the pH of sodium ethanoate (Module 6); reaction with sodium metal (author note f); soaps (chem-m7-c12); the site's pharmaceutical recall hook (site correction 1).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c08b: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue; branches amber; oxygen brick red; the carboxyl group ringed red as one functional group, its O–H hydrogen grey-white and slightly larger; δ− and δ+ small in navy; lone pairs as two small red dot pairs on O; dipole–dipole attractions dotted teal; hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dispersion forces dotted pale blue; the transferring proton in the chem-m6-c01 proton colour; the carboxylate's charge as a grey-violet glow. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Acid or alcohol?", "Name it", "Forces", "Why acidic?", "Test it"); centre the structure board, one molecule or one pair at a time; the boiling point strip at the right only in scenes 4 and 5; plates small or medium at the left or right only in scenes 1, 8, 10 and 15. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous case leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 27 Oct by contact sheet): `m6-vinegar-bottle-v1.png` (amber vinegar bottle, cork cap; scene 1, small); `m6-litmus-red-v1.png` (a red strip on a white tile; the end state in scene 8); `m6-clip-baking-soda-vinegar-before-v1.png` and `m6-clip-baking-soda-vinegar-fizz-v1.png` (aligned pair, same alpha bounds: a glass beaker of clear liquid with a heap of white powder at the base, then the same with bubbles; scene 10 and feedback 2). Not used: `m6-litmus-blue-v1.png` (shows a red-to-blue result with a red tip, wrong for this video); `m6-baking-soda-box-v1.png` (the beaker pair already shows the solid); `p01-mg-ribbon-v1.png` (the magnesium line is a short equation; a plate would add a fourth bright object).
